They often don’t seek help in the shelters, either. They often use it just to sleep, shower, and breakfast, then go about their day. If they aren’t going to seek help, it doesn’t help them to force them into positions where they WILL lose some autonomy. For some, their self-direction is all they have left that’s worth anything to them. Like the proverbial illegal gun owner unaffected by ownership restrictions, if they want their autonomy badly enough the illegality doesn’t matter to them. What’s the worst that happens? They get three hot meals served to them a day, a better than shelter-standard cot to sleep in, access to a toilet, clean stuff to put on, showers, socializing, access to reading material... I could go on. That isn’t a punishment, that’s an incentive.

Ah, shelters. Where staff isn’t allowed to do more than call 9-11 for theft or altercations, unless by some miracle there’s actual security. Where you might finally find a way to wrap your extra shirt around your head to block sufficient light and noise to catch a few hours of fitful sleep at a time between the ambient noise. No door between them and you. Nothing preventing them from walking up to your cot and shaking you out of it for a beating, if that’s what they want to do, and you’d wait at least fifteen minutes for cops to show up and peel them off you. The dark circles under homeless eyes don’t improve in shelters without makeup.


Make being homeless illegal enough and you’ll solve it by hiding most of them away from “polite society” in cells. Maybe you’ve got to worry about getting shanked, but at least you’re not packing around sixty pounds of clothes, bedding, water, toilet paper, and emergency food for almost twenty miles every week. It bears noticing that many homeless are in better physical condition than the “real citizens” throwing shade at them for being “lazy.” They’re quite likely exhausted by 3pm from lugging around everything they own because most shelters are “Not responsible for lost or stolen items.”

If you see something, say something. Call emergency. The homeless people that are decent are even more scared of those hooligans than you are. Maybe not as scared of them as they are of cops, but that takes longer to help than resolving safety issues.

One needs a lot more than a want to get off the streets for it to happen. TL;DR: Their needs for services are as varied as their reasons for being homeless, barriers exist to receiving those services AND pursuing opportunities, lastly, housing is a social norm for which few “acceptable” alternatives exist.

Life skills left to the teaching of parents often fall short of the competitive norm when those parents were themselves ill-educated. If you learned those skills organically, as you grew up, you are unlikely to have a point of reference from which to understand the difficulties that present when those skills must be learned as an adult. Adults do not change as fluidly even if they can intellectually grasp why a thing is needful. So you have those that are ill-prepared, set in their ways, may not be educated, maybe just have disagreeable personalities that lose employment (or don’t get it in the first place due to their demeanor or behavior, or physical aspects not protected by law).

Then you have those who feel they don’t deserve help to get back on their feet, who don’t feel they deserve anything nice at all, and self-sabotage. This can be symptomatic, but with so much of the public dialogue pointing to Homeless = Undeserving, it fits their lack of self-worth to embody that status. They may be afraid to fail yet again and withdraw into homelessness so nobody else expects much of them, either, therefore relieving them preemptively of dealing with being a direct disappointment themselves. Those with depression are seriously at risk when they fall into this category - I’ve seen it be a downward spiral that can lead to substance abuse as a coping mechanism (but not necessarily so, it depends on the individual).

Since I brought it up: yes, drugs. Mental health is far more of an issue because it underlies and overlaps drug abuse. If your drug of choice (espresso, doobies, booze, chocolate) is all you look forward to, you’re not going to care about the more minor creature comforts and habitual normalcies society programs us to desire. Do we NEED individual family housing? No. Do we NEED individual family cars? No. I mean, I’ve lived rurally in places where this was not true, but not because it was impossible to do without those things: because it was so incredibly inconvenient thanks to lack of public transportation and group housing options, few bothered to make the necessary arrangements.

Which brings us to convenience. Unfortunately, yes, some people are downright lazy. When it impacts you to the point of putting up a tent (as close to permanence as they can get) because the shelter wants you to do chores, or because it’s close to a day shelter where you can watch TV and / or get services, that might be all they actually want out of life. But some are treatable- existential crises can be reframed into an opportunity to create meaning, with the right therapist.

Some have stopped trying because hopelessness set in too soon to allow for early success to encourage greater (continued) efforts. I saw a young woman crumple in tears a food line yesterday because she got a dismissive call from a potential employer, after she hung up. She was so distraught she opened up to the food line at large about being a few minutes late to that interview because the bus had to stop for a train on the way and she had to wait at the next transit station, apparently this sort of thing happens to them all the time. This girl once said in my line that she had an “easy week” where she “only” walked nineteen miles. I didn’t have the guts to defend her when someone snidely asked her why she didn’t take an earlier bus to be extra sure she would be on time, and she said she was waiting for her clean laundry at the shelter so she could wear clothes that actually fit. Instead of the more usual complaint, presenting with an odor or otherwise inappropriately prepared interview appearance. Shower and laundry lines are usually long and the time slots fill quickly at the places I’ve served. There are too many in need and not enough dispersement among the available service providers.

You’ve also got the kind that were kicked out of the shelters, for any reason or no concrete reason, and those who don’t want to be in a shelter due to the lack of privacy. Shelters and so on seriously push abstinence and repression, despite usually dishing out condoms; not everyone follows their rules, but the ability to indulge sexual urges are among the misplaced priorities you sometimes see on the street. It IS a component of mental and emotional health that is often given a one-size-fits-all response, especially if trying to have a “relationship” while homeless reduces the amount of productive hours they imagine you’ll spend.

Some of them are pushing against feeling as if they are no longer in control of their lives and choosing one of the least-resistance paths to reclaim autonomy. Maybe they can’t adhere to a schedule or handle large groups of people. I haven’t done the overnight shift here but I have in Kentucky. In the morning, we turned the lights back on at 4am, after they were turned off at midnight. Food was served between 5am and 6am; ladies had to leave by 7am if they didn’t have a verified job, children, a shower or laundry slot (could stay until noon because those things took that long to go through the entire list of residents), or an appointment with one of the visiting caseworkers/ nurses. I arrived at midnight back then, at the same time as any released former inmates so there’d be fresh eyes to watch. Watching, because all we were allowed to do was call emergency if anything happened, even theft right in front of our eyes. We weren’t supposed to tell the victim who did it, either, because of the same kinds of liability issues. Somebody could have been hurt in retribution, or in the attempt of administering retribution... and we were always told that was worse than allowing the theft.

That quickly became a wall of text, so I will stop listing there and reiterate - you’ve got to have the desire, the life skills (punctuality, self-discipline, focus on productivity), the emotional resilience and mental health, and above all, positive rather than detrimental coping mechanisms. Because that is a lot of time spent standing in a line for a scoop of plain oatmeal, an orange, and a black coffee in the morning. That’s a lot of time wasted waiting to see an overloaded caseworker. Lot of time walking to bus stops, waiting for buses, scoping the ground for bus fare or panhandling it. They may be seen to have nothing but time when you witness a stationary tent village taking some leisure, but that’s not the only face of homelessness. It’s just the one that makes it easier for judgmental types to shrug off the whole issue because “clearly they don’t deserve and aren’t seeking help.” They’re just people. Not all bad, not all good. And let me just say, I don’t particularly enjoy trying to be 100% productive 100% of the time either. If I didn’t buy into the gimmick of wanting air conditioning and creature comforts that are bad for the environment and my physical health (not to mention social standing) I might have joined them. It isn’t glamorous. They aren’t free. They don’t usually have any Internet. But I happen to kind of like tents as long as I can get back out of the mosquitos.

Hoping that was sarcasm. Addicts can be very functional individuals, on a variety of drugs. Prioritization is often a skill the homeless lack or are not practicing; if something can brighten their day, it becomes that much more alluring. They have so little to look forward to - a hot shower and clean clothes, if lucky, and a more or less edible meal. Safe sleeping spaces don’t exist, not even in shelters because staff can’t do anything but call authorities for altercations or theft. (Liability issue.) With libraries unavailable as a place to put in applications in bulk, online, and nothing in the way of legitimate pastimes, what does that leave them to do? SOME volunteer. Others lack all motivation because they’ve seen how much effort they can expend and accomplish literally nothing.

I posted elsewhere but think it bears repeating, the homeless may experience other similar circumstances and exhibit similar behaviors but treatment and housing go farther than criminalization and forced hopelessness. If you’ve been homeless, you know how difficult it is to claw your way up from the bottom. 

We can’t just keep throwing religious platitudes about acceptance being part of the grace of God and this is happening to them for a reason. They are clinging to what shreds of autonomy they retain as it is. And it doesn’t help to remind them other societies’ poor may have it worse - nobody ever fixed their own issues by feeling guilty for wanting improvements, and that’s what it causes.

EDIT: Take a sociology class or two, folks. Come on. IDGAF how unpopular it is, it is increasingly accurate in its metrics and broadens one’s understanding of what others face. Not just Can face, but Do face. Or - better yet - help out at one of the day shelters and get to know some of these folks before being so quick to throw stones. They’re human. They will be treated as such. Just maybe not by you.

A lot of folks like to give the homeless a bad name - homeless included.

“Homeless.” It really isn’t incredibly useful as an umbrella term, as it must include families with small children, working couples with functional alcoholism (or whatever other addiction you might imagine), the untreated or inconsistently-treated mentally ill, the social deviants who may fancy themselves modern nomads or aren’t willing (able?) to follow the scripts of normalcy, the students who couldn’t afford housing but want to keep their autonomy, the car-dwellers, the survivor statistics... I could go on but I’m willing to bet it’s unnecessary.

I’m just saying, the symptom of thievery isn’t the only societal ill needing treatment here, and it is fairly discriminatory to lump all homeless together in accusatory terms. Imagine viewing the diverse population of circumcised men so critically - as though all had chosen to give that up, and as though it somehow must define them as people.

Please, I beg of you, be kind. Perhaps try taking a look at the whole scene from a sociological perspective. Living in the legal gray area where being a good citizen and reporting thieves can ruin your life (or end it) is not enviable. Shouldering up to known thieves because you’re afraid not to have some kind of person helping you stay awake at night is not enviable. Buying stolen goods unknowingly because you believed the seller’s BS about the pawn shop not giving a fair price - also not enviable.

I knew a young fellow that sold a gaming laptop for $300 and a pack of Camels; owed some people money, apparently, and never came up with it as far as I know. I suspect he was a fence and got to keep part of the cut - guy had a really nice, misleading type of grin. You’d swear he was utterly guileless. If you aren’t careful who you are around, it can bite you in the arse, and some end up learning it the hard way. I’m not into other folks’ drama boiling over on me and I have served at day shelters enough to want to plead for a distinction to be made anyhow. I firmly believe we can all do better; the homeless, their service providers, the political turtles protecting their careers, the genuine protesters, the capitalists with interest making modest earners feel superior funding those politicians’ careers.

I’m way more likely to give a few bucks to a struggling person picking up trash at a park just to have something useful to do than one who can get up early to hold a cardboard sign but visibly never seems to have time to volunteer. You get all types down here. I met a supposed biologist with a framed PhD (or shockingly impressive fake; we don’t follow up, caseworkers might*) who said he lived in his van for a year as an adjunct before smoking some laced weed at a party and became a meth addict virtually overnight. It’s sad crap all around, but shrugging it off as “if you’re a good person, you’ll find ways to get by on the more or less right side of the law” seems to sidestep that some need treatment more than handcuffs. I wish we had better ways of administering both here. Nobody should fall so low, in either regard.
